section_summary: This section examines Japan’s postwar trade deficit, dependence on U.S. aid, and the effects of the Dodge economic stabilization program. U.S. and British officials report on inflation, credit, exchange rates, export controls, and trade negotiations. Later documents present the Economic Stabilization Board’s and Social Democratic Party’s concerns about deflation, unemployment, and the distribution of the program’s costs.

subfiles.title: Survey of Japan’s Economic Problems, with Foreign Trade Appendices
subfiles.from: E. R. Lingeman, Economic Adviser’s Office, United Kingdom Liaison Mission, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A British economic survey assesses Japan’s trade, inflation, stabilization measures, U.S. aid, and prospects for self-support.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages discuss Japan’s import needs, export obstacles, and persistent trade deficit. Lingeman credits Dodge’s austerity measures with slowing inflation but warns that tight credit and weak world markets complicate recovery. He doubts Japan can become self-supporting by 1953 without substantial U.S. assistance. Four appendices tabulate foreign trade, imports, exports, and trade with the Sterling Area.

subfiles.title: Comments on Status of Nine Point Economic Stabilization Program in Japan
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The mission forwards Sherwood Fine’s comments on a State Department study and assesses Japanese resistance to stabilization.
subfiles.summary: Fine considers the study broadly sound but criticizes the Yoshida Cabinet’s cooperation. The mission finds resistance less coordinated than Fine suggests and reports views from SCAP and Japanese officials on austerity, public works, and the program’s progress.

subfiles.title: Status of the Economic Stabilization Program
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: An enclosed report reviews prices, wages, unemployment, exports, budgets, credit, and taxation under stabilization.
subfiles.summary: The report describes greater price and wage stability following the nine-point directive and Dodge Mission recommendations. It reviews subsidy and price-control changes, unemployment, the export outlook, budget management, banking credit, and tax collections. It concludes that stabilization has advanced, while inflationary risks and the need for industrial rationalization remain.

subfiles.title: Progress on the Nine-Point Economic Stabilization Program
subfiles.from: Economic and Scientific Section, General Headquarters, SCAP
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: A SCAP progress statement reviews implementation of the nine stabilization directives.
subfiles.summary: The statement covers the balanced budget, tax enforcement, credit and wage restraints, price controls, export promotion, raw-material use, and food distribution.

subfiles.title: Weekly Economic Affairs Airgram A-256
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A weekly airgram reports discussions of Japanese economic policy, trade, investment, and occupation administration.
subfiles.summary: Topics include the tobacco monopoly, housing for occupation personnel, SCAP management, Japanese cooperation with stabilization, raw-material purchasing, and trade with the Sterling Area and Pakistan.

subfiles.title: Export Associations and Floor Prices
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department questions a Japanese proposal to restore private export associations after abolition of floor prices.
subfiles.summary: Warns that private associations could restrict competition, fix prices, and hinder exports; requests comments.

subfiles.title: Weekly Economic Affairs Airgram A-267
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The mission reports developments in coal procurement, export administration, investment, and Sterling Area trade.
subfiles.summary: The airgram reports that Japan cannot presently buy much Kailan coking coal despite the supplier’s interest. It also discusses copper shipments, foreign trade representation, planned changes to import and export controls, and Sterling Area negotiations.

subfiles.title: Weekly Economic Affairs Airgram A-276
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The mission reports on proposed trade reforms, the yen-dollar rate, foreign investment, and procurement policy.
subfiles.summary: A U.S. advisory mission favors removing export floor prices, while SCAP announces that it does not contemplate yen devaluation. Other items concern Sovexportfilm, suspended deconcentration orders, Japanese export-pricing proposals, private imports, Korean trade, Sterling Area payments, and raw-material procurement.

subfiles.title: Turnover of Economic Responsibilities for Japan to ECA
subfiles.about: The memorandum weighs transferring the Army’s Japanese recovery responsibilities to the Economic Cooperation Administration.
subfiles.summary: Fearey sees advantages in an ECA takeover around July 1950 but advises sounding out Army and SCAP before proceeding. He also recommends appropriation language permitting a later transfer of aid funds.

subfiles.title: Summary of Tokyo Despatch 679
subfiles.about: A State Department note summarizes Lingeman’s British assessment of Japan’s economy and the Dodge Mission.
subfiles.summary: Highlights U.S. aid, rapid stabilization gains, and doubts about self-support by 1953.

subfiles.title: Record Copy Replacement Notice
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: The form designates a replacement record copy for an action copy not returned to central records.
subfiles.summary: Directs return of the replacement copy for filing.

subfiles.title: Weekly Economic Affairs Airgram A-282
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The mission reports on restituted narcotics, Soviet commercial status, trade agreements, investment, and stockpiles.
subfiles.summary: The airgram describes efforts to sell restituted opium, Japanese consideration of Sovexportfilm’s legal status, and debates over wheat purchases and Netherlands-Indonesian trade. It also notes proposed foreign investments and disagreement over whether Japan should acquire more import stockpiles.

subfiles.title: Views of Social Democratic Party and Economic Stabilization Board with Regard to Economic Stabilization
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch explains opposition proposals for easing the deflationary effects of the Dodge Line.
subfiles.summary: Sebald contrasts the Finance Ministry’s restrictive approach with the Economic Stabilization Board’s call for more investment, public works, and credit within a balanced budget. He summarizes arguments by Wada Hiroo, Inaba Hidezo, and Tsuru Shigeto about unemployment, real wages, and Japanese responsibility for recovery. He suggests that the Social Democratic Party may favor broader relaxation of the Dodge Line than it openly acknowledges.

subfiles.title: Divergent Views on Implementation of Economic Stabilization Program
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum compares two proposed routes to Japanese economic stabilization.
subfiles.summary: Felsenthal outlines assumptions behind the Economic Stabilization Board’s 1953 targets for production, trade, and productivity. Plan A emphasizes eliminating inflation and restraining public investment; Plan B proposes gradual investment expansion, easier credit, public works, and use of aid counterpart funds.

subfiles.title: What We Hope for from Mr. Dodge — Wada Hiroo
subfiles.about: Wada argues that the Yoshida government’s implementation of the Dodge program burdens workers and small enterprises.
subfiles.summary: He calls for less debt redemption, more public works and unemployment relief, tax relief, and timely use of the Counterpart Fund. He urges policies that spread the costs of stabilization and improve ordinary livelihoods.

subfiles.title: What We Hope for from Mr. Dodge — Inaba Hidezo
subfiles.about: Inaba assesses signs of stagnation and hidden unemployment in Japan’s economy.
subfiles.summary: Cites falling production, growing stocks and debts, and employment losses as reasons to reconsider current policy.
